t:
(a) In General.—Section 7703(b) of title 5, United States Code, is amended by striking the matter preceding paragraph (2) and inserting the following:“(b)(1)(A) Except as provided in subparagraph (B) and paragraph (2) of this subsection, a petition to review a final order or final decision of the Board shall be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any petition for review shall be filed within 60 days after the Board issues notice of the final order or decision of the Board.“(B) During the 2-year period beginning on the effective date of the Whistleblower Protection Enhancement Act of 2012, a petition to review a final order or final decision of the Board that raises no challenge to the Board’s disposition of allegations of a prohibited personnel practice described in section 2302(b) other than practices described in section 2302(b)(8), or 2302(b)(9) (A)(i), (B), (C), or (D) shall be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit or any court of appeals of competent jurisdiction. Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any petition for review shall be filed within 60 days after the Board issues notice of the final order or decision of the Board.”. 
    (b) Review Obtained by Office of Personnel Management.—Section 7703(d) of title 5, United States Code, is amended to read as follows:“(d)(1) Except as provided under paragraph (2), this paragraph shall apply to any review obtained by the Director of the Office of Personnel Management. The Director may obtain review of any final order or decision of the Board by filing, within 60 days after the Board issues notice of the final order or decision of the Board, a petition for judicial review in the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit if the Director determines, in the discretion of the Director, that the Board erred in interpreting a civil service law, rule, or regulation affecting personnel management and that the Board’s decision will have a substantial impact on a civil service law, rule, regulation, or policy directive. If the Director did not intervene in a matter before the Board, the Director may not petition for review of a Board decision under this section unless 
the Director first petitions the Board for a reconsideration of its decision, and such petition is denied. In addition to the named respondent, the Board and all other parties to the proceedings before the Board shall have the right to appear in the proceeding before the Court of Appeals. The granting of the petition for judicial review shall be at the discretion of the Court of Appeals.“(2) During the 2-year period beginning on the effective date of the Whistleblower Protection Enhancement Act of 2012, this paragraph shall apply to any review obtained by the Director of the Office of Personnel Management that raises no challenge to the Board’s disposition of allegations of a prohibited personnel practice described in section 2302(b) other than practices described in section 2302(b)(8), or 2302(b)(9) (A)(i), (B), (C), or (D). The Director may obtain review of any final order or decision of the Board by filing, within 60 days after the Board issues notice of the final order or decision of the Board, a petition for judicial review in the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit or any court of appeals of competent jurisdiction if the Director determines, in the discretion of the Director, that the Board erred in interpreting a civil service law, rule, or regulation affecting personnel management and that the Board’s decision will have a substantial impact on a civil service law, rule, regulation, or policy directive. If the Director did not intervene in a matter before the Board, the Director may not petition for review of a Board decision under this section unless the Director first petitions the Board for a reconsideration of its decision, and such petition is denied. In addition to the named respondent, the Board and all other parties to the proceedings before the Board shall have the right to appear in the proceeding before the court of appeals. The granting of the petition for judicial review shall be at the discretion of the court of appeals.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that "petition to review" grants a right to sue the government over a decision. But this section only sets venue (Federal Circuit or another court of appeals) and the 60-day filing deadline for review of Merit Systems Protection Board decisions, and describes when the Director of OPM, a federal official, may seek review. Describing venue and time limits is not the same as granting an outside party a new right to sue, and the actors here are federal employees and officials in personnel disputes rather than outside parties consulted on a federal policy decision.
fable.s: a petition to review a final order or final decision of the Board shall be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit or any court of appeals of competent jurisdiction

opus.w: Subsection (a) only sets which court hears petitions to review Merit Systems Protection Board decisions and the 60-day filing deadline. The definition excludes venue and deadline rules because they describe litigation rather than grant a new right to sue. Subsection (b) gives the right to seek review to the Director of the Office of Personnel Management, a federal official, so it stays inside the government. The clause letting other parties appear only covers people already in the case, who are mostly federal agencies and employees, in a review the Director has started, so it does not bring outsiders into a federal decision.
opus.s: a petition to review a final order or final decision of the Board shall be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any petition for review shall be filed within 60 days after the Board issues notice of the final order or decision of the Board.
opus.b:
I'm labelling this **No**, with moderate confidence (0.7).

**The tempting reading:** The section is about filing petitions to court to review Merit Systems Protection Board decisions. The definition counts the ability to sue over a decision as participation, so this looks like a Yes at first.

**Why that reading fails:**
- **Subsection (a)** doesn't create a right to sue. That right already exists in 5 U.S.C. 7703(a). This amendment only sets which court hears the petition (the Federal Circuit, or for two years any competent court of appeals) and the 60-day filing deadline. The definition lists venue and deadlines as a "No" trap.
- **Subsection (b)** gives the right to seek review to the Director of the Office of Personnel Management, who is a federal official. A federal official asking a court to review a federal board's decision stays inside the government.
- **"All other parties ... shall have the right to appear"** is the strongest hook for a Yes. But the parties before the Board are typically federal agencies and federal employees or applicants. And this clause only lets them appear in a review the Director has already started; it doesn't give outsiders a new right to sue.

**The main risk:** Employees or applicants who appeal to the Board may count as outside parties. On that reading, the right-to-appear clause could support a Yes, which is why confidence is not higher.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes the venue (United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit) and the statute of limitations (60 days) for filing petitions for judicial review. According to the definition, describing court jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits is not the same as granting an outside party a right to sue or requiring participation in a decision-making process. It regulates the procedural aspects of existing litigation rights rather than creating a new participatory mechanism like consultation or public comment.
qwen_chat.s: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any petition for review shall be filed within 60 days after the Board issues notice of the final order or decision of the Board.
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: The section mentions "any petition for review" and "all other parties to the proceedings," which might suggest that outside parties (like whistleblowers) have a right to sue or participate in the judicial review process. However, the definition explicitly states that "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits - limiting or describing litigation is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue a decision." Furthermore, the specific actors granted the right to petition for review in this text are the "Director of the Office of Personnel Management" (a federal official) and implicitly the parties to the administrative proceeding, but the text itself is primarily establishing the procedural mechanism (venue and timing) for judicial review rather than creating a new participatory right for the general public or outside entities to influence the initial federal decision. The key distinction is that this section defines *how* and *where* existing legal challenges are filed, not a consultation or coordination process before a decision is made. The "parties" mentioned are those already involved in the administrative case, not new outside participants being consulted.

Actually, looking closer at the definition: "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision." The text says "a petition to review a final order... shall be filed". This grants the right to seek judicial review. Who can file? Subsection (a) says "a petition... shall be filed". It doesn't explicitly restrict it to the Director in (a), but (b) specifically grants the Director the right. Usually, the aggrieved party (the employee/whistleblower) is the one filing. Is an employee "outside" the federal government? Yes, generally. However, the definition trap says: "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits - limiting or describing litigation is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue a decision." This section is amending the venue and timing (60 days) for petitions. It is describing the litigation process. It is not *granting* the right to sue; the right to sue is likely established elsewhere (e.g., in the Whistleblower Protection Act itself). This section just says *where* and *when* you file. Therefore, it falls under the "No" trap for describing litigation procedures.
